sections.title: 1. Anti-Money Laundering (AML) Framework
sections.overview: Money laundering is the process of disguising illicit proceeds to make them appear legitimate. Broker-dealers must establish written AML programs under the Bank Secrecy Act as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act, with FinCEN as the primary administering bureau. FINRA Rule 3310 codifies the BD AML compliance obligation.
key_concepts: Three stages of laundering: Placement (introducing illicit cash into the financial system), Layering (disguising the trail through complex transactions), Integration (returning funds to the launderer as apparently legitimate wealth).
Structuring (a.k.a. smurfing): breaking transactions into amounts below the $10,000 CTR threshold to evade reporting — itself a federal crime.

Required AML program elements (five pillars): (1) written policies/procedures, (2) designated AML Compliance Officer, (3) ongoing employee training, (4) independent testing (annual for most firms), (5) risk-based Customer Due Diligence (CDD)/beneficial-owner identification.
Customer Identification Program (CIP) under PATRIOT Act §326: collect name, DOB, physical address, and taxpayer ID (SSN/TIN); verify identity within a reasonable time; check against government lists.
Currency Transaction Report (CTR / FinCEN Form 112): filed for cash transactions exceeding $10,000 in a single day (aggregated). Applies to currency only — not checks or wires.

Suspicious Activity Report (SAR / FinCEN Form 111): filed within 30 calendar days of detection (60 days if no suspect identified); $5,000 threshold; STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL — disclosure to the subject is prohibited.
FinCEN: bureau of the U.S. Treasury that administers the BSA and receives CTRs/SARs.
OFAC: enforces economic sanctions; maintains the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List; firms must screen customers and block prohibited transactions.
PATRIOT Act §314(a): law enforcement information requests to financial institutions. §314(b): voluntary information sharing among financial institutions.
rules: FINRA Rule 3310 — AML compliance program requirements.
USA PATRIOT Act §326 — CIP requirements.
USA PATRIOT Act §352 — required AML program.
USA PATRIOT Act §314 — cooperative information sharing.
formulas: CTR trigger: aggregate same-day cash in/out > $10,000
SAR filing deadline: file within 30 days of detection (+30 day extension if suspect unknown, max 60 days)
mnemonics: PLI = Placement, Layering, Integration (laundering stages).
CIP minimum data = 'NAID': Name, Address, ID number (TIN), Date of birth.
AML 5 pillars = 'PORT-I': Policies, Officer (AMLCO), tRaining, Testing (independent), Identification (CDD).

sections.title: 2. Market Manipulation
sections.overview: Market manipulation comprises intentional acts that distort the natural forces of supply and demand to mislead other market participants. Exchange Act §10(b) and Rule 10b-5 are the broad anti-fraud/anti-manipulation provisions; FINRA Rules 2020, 5210, 5220, 5230, 5240, 5270, 5280, and 5290 implement specific prohibitions.
key_concepts: Pump-and-dump: artificially inflating a thinly traded security's price via false promotion, then selling into the demand.
Front running: trading ahead of a known customer block order (FINRA Rule 5270).

Trading ahead of customer orders (Rule 5320 / 'Manning rule'): a firm holding a customer limit order generally may not trade for its own account at the same or better price without filling the customer.
Marking the close / marking the open: entering trades at session boundaries to influence reported price or benchmark.
Painting the tape / matched orders / wash trades: coordinated trades creating false appearance of activity.
Spreading false rumors (Rule 5270/2020): communicating unverified market-moving information to affect price.
Backing away (Rule 5220): a market maker's failure to honor its firm quotation.
Freeriding: buying securities without intent or ability to pay, then selling to cover the original purchase.
Excessive trading / churning: trading in a customer account primarily to generate commissions, inconsistent with the customer's objectives.
Quotations must be bona fide (Rule 5210); fictitious quotes prohibited.
Influencing or rewarding employees of others (Rule 3220 / Rule 3240 — gifts and borrowing) is separately restricted to prevent quid-pro-quo manipulation.
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §10(b) — manipulative/deceptive devices.
17 CFR 240.10b-5 — employment of manipulative and deceptive devices.
17 CFR 240.10b-3 — manipulative practices by brokers/dealers.
17 CFR 240.15c1-2 — fraud and misrepresentation.
FINRA Rule 2020 — use of manipulative, deceptive, or other fraudulent devices.
FINRA Rule 5210 — publication of transactions and quotations.
FINRA Rule 5220 — offers at stated prices (no backing away).
FINRA Rule 5230 — payments involving publications that influence the market.
FINRA Rule 5240 — anti-intimidation/coordination.
FINRA Rule 5270 — front running of block transactions.
FINRA Rule 5280 — trading ahead of research reports.
FINRA Rule 5290 — order entry and execution practices.
FINRA Rule 5310 — best execution.
FINRA Rule 5320 — prohibition against trading ahead of customer orders.
mnemonics: Manipulation acts = 'FM-PAW-BC': Front-running, Marking the close, Pump-and-dump, Painting the tape, Wash trades, Backing away, Churning.

sections.title: 3. Insider Trading — MNPI
sections.overview: Insider trading is the purchase or sale of a security in breach of a fiduciary duty or other relationship of trust while in possession of material, nonpublic information (MNPI). Liability extends to tippers, tippees, and misappropriators. Penalties were dramatically expanded by ITSA (1984) and ITSFEA (1988).
key_concepts: Material information: information a reasonable investor would consider important to an investment decision (e.g., earnings surprises, M&A, FDA approval, executive change).
Nonpublic: not yet broadly disseminated to the marketplace.
Classical theory: corporate insider (officer, director, employee, controlling shareholder) trades on MNPI in breach of duty to shareholders.
Misappropriation theory: outsider (attorney, banker, printer) trades on MNPI in breach of duty owed to the source.
Tipper/tippee liability: tipper must receive a personal benefit; tippee inherits the duty when she knows or should know of the breach.
Rule 10b5-1: 'on the basis of' means aware of MNPI at the time of trade; affirmative-defense trading plans must be adopted in good faith when not aware of MNPI.
Rule 10b5-2: enumerated relationships creating duty of trust/confidence in misappropriation cases (e.g., agreement of confidentiality; history/pattern of confidences; certain family relationships).
Civil penalties (§21A): up to 3x profit gained or loss avoided ('treble damages'); controlling persons up to greater of $1,000,000 or 3x.
Criminal penalties: up to $5,000,000 fine and 20 years imprisonment for individuals (per ITSFEA, as amended); up to $25,000,000 for entities.
Private right of action (§20A): contemporaneous traders may sue; damages capped at violator's profit gained/loss avoided; 5-year statute of limitations.
SROs may impose bars, suspensions, and fines; SEC may seek disgorgement and injunctions.
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §10(b).
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §20A — contemporaneous-trader private action.
Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §21A — civil penalties for insider trading.
17 CFR 240.10b-5 — anti-fraud rule.
17 CFR 240.10b5-1 — 'on the basis of' definition; trading plans.
17 CFR 240.10b5-2 — duties in misappropriation cases.
formulas: Civil penalty cap = 3 × (profit gained OR loss avoided)
Controlling-person penalty = greater of $1,000,000 OR 3 × controlled person's profit/loss avoided
§20A private damages ≤ defendant's profit gained or loss avoided; SOL = 5 years
mnemonics: MNPI test = 'MN': Material AND Nonpublic.
Penalty triangle = 'F-I-D': Fines (treble/$5M), Imprisonment (20 yrs), Disgorgement.

sections.title: 4. Restricted Persons & IPO Allocations (Rule 5130 / 5131)
sections.overview: FINRA prohibits broker-dealers from selling new equity issues (IPOs of common stock) to industry insiders to preserve the integrity of the public offering process. Rule 5130 covers 'restricted persons'; Rule 5131 addresses 'spinning' and other allocation abuses involving executives of public/covered companies.
key_concepts: Covered offering: equity IPO of a common stock at the public offering price (does not apply to debt, investment-company shares, or follow-on/secondary offerings).

Restricted persons include: FINRA members; broker-dealer employees and their immediate family members (spouse, parents, in-laws, siblings, children — where the BD employee materially supports or is supported by them, or has authority/control over the account); finders and fiduciaries with respect to the offering; portfolio managers buying for personal account; persons owning 10%+ of a BD.
Immediate family exception: aunts/uncles, grandparents, and other relatives are generally NOT restricted.
Pre-allocation requirement: BD must obtain (within prior 12 months) a written representation from the account that it is eligible to receive new issues.
Rule 5131 — 'spinning': prohibits allocating new issues to executive officers/directors of companies that are existing/prospective investment-banking clients in exchange for business (quid pro quo).
Rule 5131 also restricts flipping, market-order policies, and IPO 'pricing/trading practices' on the day of effectiveness.
rules: FINRA Rule 5130 — restrictions on the purchase and sale of IPOs of equity securities.
FINRA Rule 5131 — new issue allocations and distributions (spinning).
mnemonics: Restricted = 'BD-FFP-10': Broker-Dealers, Finders/Fiduciaries, Family of BD employees (immediate), Portfolio managers, 10% owners of BDs.

sections.title: 5. Senior & Specified-Adult Protections (Rule 2165 / 4512 Trusted Contact)
sections.overview: FINRA's senior-investor framework targets financial exploitation of older and impaired adults via two coordinated rules: Rule 4512 (trusted contact person required at account opening) and Rule 2165 (temporary holds on disbursements and on transactions where exploitation is suspected).
key_concepts: Specified adult: a natural person aged 65 or older; OR a natural person 18+ whom the firm reasonably believes has a mental or physical impairment rendering him/her unable to protect his/her own interests.

Trusted Contact Person (TCP): firms must make reasonable effort to obtain name and contact information of a TCP at account opening (or by the next account update for existing accounts). TCP is not a power-of-attorney and cannot trade.

Rule 2165 temporary hold — DISBURSEMENTS: firm may place a hold on a suspected exploitative disbursement for up to 15 business days; may extend internally an additional 10 business days (total 25 business days); a state regulator/agency/court may extend by 30 additional business days (total 55 business days).
Rule 2165 temporary hold — TRANSACTIONS (effective 3/17/2022): hold authority now also extends to securities transactions, not only cash disbursements (Reg. Notice 22-05).
Notification required: firm must promptly notify all parties authorized to transact (other than the suspected exploiter) and the trusted contact, and conduct an internal review.

Rule 3241: a registered person must obtain written firm approval before being named as a beneficiary, executor, trustee, or holder of POA for a customer who is not an immediate family member (effective 2/15/2021).
Diminished capacity red flags: difficulty completing routine transactions, memory loss, sudden interest in risky speculative products, isolation from family.
rules: FINRA Rule 2165 — financial exploitation of specified adults.
FINRA Rule 4512 — customer account information (trusted contact).
FINRA Rule 3241 — registered person being named as beneficiary or holding position of trust.
formulas: 2165 hold timeline: 15 BD initial + 10 BD internal extension + 30 BD agency/court extension = up to 55 business days
mnemonics: Specified adult = '65 or 18+ Impaired'.
Hold ladder = '15-25-55' business days.

sections.title: 6. Improper Use of Customer Assets
sections.overview: Registered persons may not borrow from, lend to, share in, or otherwise convert customer assets except under narrowly defined firm-approved exceptions. The customer protection rule and FINRA Rules 2150, 3240, 3260, and 3210 enforce strict segregation of customer and firm/registered-person interests.
key_concepts: Rule 2150: prohibits improper use or commingling of customer funds/securities; prohibits guarantees against loss; prohibits sharing in profits/losses of customer accounts EXCEPT with prior written firm consent AND prior written customer consent, and only in proportion to the registered person's financial contribution (immediate-family exception eliminates the proportionality requirement).

Rule 3240: borrowing from or lending to customers prohibited unless firm has written procedures permitting it AND the relationship fits a permitted category (e.g., immediate family; bank/lending institution customer in the ordinary course; personal/business relationship outside the BD relationship).
Rule 3260: discretionary accounts — written authorization required; orders must be marked discretionary; subject to frequent supervisory review.
Rule 3210: registered person must give written notice to employer firm before opening an outside brokerage account; the executing firm must provide duplicate confirms/statements upon request.
Rule 3250: prohibits accepting conditions or stipulations that limit liability for losses (no 'guarantees').
Customer protection (Exchange Act §15(c)(3) / Rule 15c3-3): segregation of fully paid and excess-margin securities; reserve formula deposit.
rules: FINRA Rule 2150 — improper use of customers' securities or funds; prohibition against guarantees and sharing.
FINRA Rule 3210 — accounts at other broker-dealers.
FINRA Rule 3240 — borrowing from or lending to customers.
FINRA Rule 3250 — prohibition on guarantees against loss.
FINRA Rule 3260 — discretionary accounts.
mnemonics: Cannot 'BLGS' with customers without firm permission: Borrow, Lend, Guarantee, Share.

sections.title: 7. Unregistered Persons — Permitted vs. Prohibited Activities
sections.overview: Only properly registered persons may solicit customers, take orders, or receive transaction-based compensation. Rule 2040 governs payments to unregistered persons; Rule 1240 covers continuing education; SEC and FINRA strictly prohibit using non-registered staff as de facto reps.
key_concepts: Unregistered (clerical) personnel MAY: respond to existing-customer inquiries about account balances, quote prices/yields from a published source, take messages, distribute pre-approved literature on request, and perform administrative tasks.
Unregistered personnel MAY NOT: solicit new business, recommend securities, take orders, discuss product features that constitute a recommendation, or receive transaction-based compensation.

Rule 2040: firms may not pay commissions/transaction-based fees to unregistered persons, except permissible continuing commissions to retired reps (under a bona fide written agreement) and certain payments to non-U.S. finders meeting strict conditions.
Rule 3270: outside business activities require prior written notice to firm.
Rule 3280: private securities transactions ('selling away') require prior written notice and, if compensated, firm approval and supervision.
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §15(a) — broker-dealer registration requirement.
FINRA Rule 2040 — payments to unregistered persons.
FINRA Rule 3270 — outside business activities.
FINRA Rule 3280 — private securities transactions.
mnemonics: Clerk CAN: Quote (published), Mail, Schedule. Clerk CAN'T: Solicit, Recommend, Take orders, Get commissions.

sections.title: 8. Communications with the Public (Rule 2210)
sections.overview: FINRA Rule 2210 classifies all communications into three categories with distinct filing, approval, and content standards. All communications must be fair, balanced, not misleading, and approved per category requirements; principal pre-use approval is generally required for retail communications.
key_concepts: Retail communication: any written (including electronic) communication distributed or made available to MORE than 25 retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period. Generally requires registered principal approval BEFORE first use.

Correspondence: any written (including electronic) communication distributed or made available to 25 OR FEWER retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period. Subject to supervision and review but not pre-use approval.

Institutional communication: written communication distributed exclusively to institutional investors (banks, RIAs, insurance companies, registered investment companies, government entities, BDs, qualified plans with $50M+, natural persons with $50M+). Not subject to pre-use principal approval but firms must have written supervisory procedures.

Filing requirements: new member firms must pre-file retail communications for first year; certain retail communications about registered investment companies, options, security futures, bond funds, etc., require filing with FINRA Advertising Regulation Department (typically within 10 business days of first use; 10 BDs before first use for some categories).

Content standards: no false/exaggerated/promissory statements; balanced discussion of risks and benefits; predictions of performance prohibited (except as permitted for certain registered offerings/IRA projections).
Required disclosures: identity of member firm; testimonials must disclose if paid >$100, that experience may not be representative, and any material conflict.
Public appearances and social media: subject to general standards; static content typically treated as retail communication; interactive content treated as correspondence.
rules: FINRA Rule 2210 — communications with the public.
FINRA Rule 2220 — options communications (parallel framework).
FINRA Rule 2264 — margin disclosure statement.
FINRA Rule 2231 — customer account statements.
FINRA Rule 2251 — processing/forwarding of proxy and other issuer-related materials.
formulas: Retail vs. Correspondence threshold = 25 retail investors / 30 calendar days
mnemonics: 3 categories = 'RIC': Retail, Institutional, Correspondence.
25/30 rule: >25 retail in 30 days = Retail; ≤25 = Correspondence.

sections.title: 9. Telemarketing & Cold-Calling (Rule 3230 / TCPA)
sections.overview: The Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA) and FINRA Rule 3230 govern outbound cold-calls to consumers, restricting hours, requiring identification, and mandating DNC list maintenance and scrubbing.
key_concepts: Permissible calling hours: 8:00 AM to 9:00 PM in the LOCAL TIME of the called party.
National Do-Not-Call (DNC) Registry: must scrub call lists against the federal registry; firms must also maintain an internal (firm-specific) DNC list.
Required disclosures on each call: caller's name, firm name, firm telephone number/address, purpose of the call (solicit purchase of securities/services).

Established business relationship exception: may call existing customers for up to 18 months after last transaction; may call after consumer's inquiry/application for 3 months — but if customer is on internal DNC list, do not call.
Written/signed consent overrides DNC.
Firms must train personnel and maintain written DNC policies and procedures.
rules: FINRA Rule 3230 — telemarketing.
formulas: Calling window = 8 AM – 9 PM local time (called party's time zone)
EBR exception: 18 months post-transaction; 3 months post-inquiry
mnemonics: '8 to 9' for time; 'NIP' disclosure = Name, Identify firm, Phone number/purpose.

sections.title: 10. Reg BI, KYC, Suitability & Form CRS
sections.overview: Regulation Best Interest (Rule 15l-1) imposes a 'best interest' standard on broker-dealer recommendations to retail customers, working with FINRA Rules 2090 (KYC) and 2111 (suitability). Form CRS (17 CFR 240.17a-14) delivers a plain-English client relationship summary.
key_concepts: Reg BI four obligations: (1) Disclosure, (2) Care, (3) Conflict of Interest, (4) Compliance.

Care Obligation: BD must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to (a) understand the recommendation (reasonable-basis), (b) have a reasonable basis to believe it is in the particular retail customer's best interest (customer-specific), and (c) ensure series of recommendations are not excessive (quantitative).
Rule 2090 (Know Your Customer): use reasonable diligence regarding every account to know the essential facts about each customer.
Rule 2111 (Suitability): applies to recommendations to non-retail customers and otherwise complements Reg BI. Three suitability components: reasonable-basis, customer-specific, quantitative.
Customer Investment Profile factors: age, other investments, financial situation/needs, tax status, investment objectives, investment experience, time horizon, liquidity needs, risk tolerance.
Form CRS (Form ADV Part 3 for advisers; Form CRS for BDs): delivered at or before earliest of (1) recommendation of account type/security/strategy, (2) placing first order, (3) opening account.
What is a 'recommendation': call to action; based on facts and circumstances; the more individually tailored, the more likely it constitutes a recommendation.
rules: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 — Regulation Best Interest.
17 CFR 240.17a-14 — Form CRS.
FINRA Rule 2090 — Know Your Customer.
FINRA Rule 2111 — Suitability.
mnemonics: Reg BI = '4 Cs': Care, Conflicts, Compliance, disClosure.
Suitability triangle = 'R-C-Q': Reasonable-basis, Customer-specific, Quantitative.

sections.title: 11. Books, Records, Confirmations & Statements
sections.overview: SEC Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4 prescribe what records BDs must create and how long they must preserve them. Customer-facing documentation — trade confirmations (Rule 10b-10) and account statements (FINRA Rule 2231) — is also strictly regulated.
key_concepts: Rule 17a-3: records to be MADE (blotters, ledgers, order tickets, customer account records, trial balances, etc.).

Rule 17a-4: records to be PRESERVED. Common periods on SIE: blotters and general ledgers — 6 years (first 2 in easily accessible location); customer account records and communications — generally 3 years (first 2 accessible); corporate charters/partnership agreements/minute books — life of firm + 3 years (lifetime); FINRA Rule 4511 requires 6-year retention for any record without a specified period.

Rule 10b-10 (Confirmations): customer must receive a written confirmation at or before completion of the transaction; must disclose trade date, settlement date, capacity (agent/principal), price, commission (if agent) or markup (in certain principal trades), and other material facts.
FINRA Rule 2231: account statements at least quarterly; monthly if there is account activity.
FINRA Rule 4512: customer account information — name, address, DOB, TIN, employment, investment objectives, signature of registered rep and principal approval; trusted contact information.
FINRA Rule 4514: signatures of convenience prohibited; pre-signed forms prohibited.

Holding of customer mail (FINRA Rule 3150): firm may hold mail up to 3 months upon written customer instructions; longer periods allowed if customer provides a legitimate purpose (e.g., extended travel/safety).
rules: 17 CFR 240.10b-10 — confirmation of transactions.
17 CFR 240.17a-3 — records to be made.
17 CFR 240.17a-4 — records to be preserved.
FINRA Rule 4511 — general books and records (6-year default).
FINRA Rule 4512 — customer account information.
FINRA Rule 4514 — authorization records.
FINRA Rule 2231 — customer account statements.
FINRA Rule 3150 — holding of customer mail.
formulas: Customer mail hold (3150) = up to 3 months (longer w/ legitimate purpose)
Account statements = quarterly minimum, monthly if activity
mnemonics: Retention '6-3-Life': 6 yrs blotters/ledgers, 3 yrs most communications, Lifetime + 3 for organizational docs.

sections.title: 12. Regulation S-P (Privacy) & Customer Information Safeguards
sections.overview: Regulation S-P protects nonpublic personal information (NPI) of consumers/customers. Firms must deliver privacy notices, allow opt-out of certain sharing, and implement safeguards. The 2024 amendments add an incident response program and customer breach-notification timeline.
key_concepts: Nonpublic Personal Information (NPI): personally identifiable financial information that is not publicly available (e.g., SSN, account number, transaction history).
Initial privacy notice: must be provided no later than the time the customer relationship is established.
Annual privacy notice: must be provided once during any 12-consecutive-month period (with limited exception for unchanged policies and no new sharing).

Opt-out right: customer must be given a reasonable opportunity (and reasonable means) to opt out before NPI is disclosed to nonaffiliated third parties (exceptions exist for service providers, joint marketing, legal compliance).
Safeguards Rule: written policies and procedures for administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect customer records and information.

2024 amendments to Reg S-P (effective compliance: large entities 12/3/2025; small entities 6/3/2026): require (a) a written incident response program, (b) customer notification within 30 days of detecting unauthorized access/use of sensitive customer information, and (c) enhanced oversight of third-party service providers.
Disposal Rule: proper disposal of consumer report information to prevent unauthorized access.
rules: Regulation S-P (17 CFR Part 248) — privacy of consumer financial information.
FINRA Rule 3110 — supervision (extends to safeguarding policies).
formulas: Reg S-P breach notification = within 30 days of awareness of unauthorized access/use
mnemonics: Reg S-P triad = 'NOS': Notice (initial + annual), Opt-out, Safeguards.

sections.title: 13. Business Continuity Plan (BCP) — Rule 4370
sections.overview: FINRA Rule 4370 requires every member firm to create and maintain a written business continuity plan reasonably designed to enable the firm to meet existing obligations to customers in the event of an emergency or significant business disruption.
key_concepts: BCP must address at minimum: data backup and recovery; mission-critical systems; financial and operational assessments; alternate communications with customers, employees, and regulators; alternate physical location of employees; critical business constituent, bank, and counter-party impact; regulatory reporting; how the firm will assure customers prompt access to funds and securities.

Two emergency contact persons: firm must designate and report to FINRA two contact persons (both registered principals; one may be an executive officer/operations officer if the firm has only one registered principal).
BCP disclosure: firm must disclose its BCP in writing to customers at account opening, post it on its website (if any), and mail it upon request.
Annual review: senior management must review the BCP annually and update as necessary.
rules: FINRA Rule 4370 — Business Continuity Plans and Emergency Contact Information.
mnemonics: BCP review = annual; 2 emergency contacts (both principals).

sections.title: 14. Falsifying Records, Signatures of Convenience & Regulatory Cooperation
sections.overview: Integrity of books, records, and regulatory inquiry processes is foundational. FINRA Rules 2010, 4511, 4514, and 8210 (regulatory information requests) impose strict honesty and recordkeeping duties; falsification or non-response leads to severe discipline including bars.
key_concepts: Rule 2010: standards of commercial honor and just and equitable principles of trade — the catch-all ethical standard.
Rule 4511: members must make and preserve books and records as required under FINRA rules, the Exchange Act, and applicable Exchange Act rules.
Rule 4514: prohibits use of pre-signed forms and signatures of convenience.

Rule 8210 (regulatory information requests): firms and associated persons must provide information, testimony, and documents upon FINRA's written request; failure to respond is itself a violation typically resulting in suspension or bar.
Rule 2120: prohibits use of manipulative, deceptive, or fraudulent devices (parallel to Exchange Act §10(b)).
Falsifying records, altering documents, backdating, or providing misleading information to regulators violates Rule 2010 and may also violate the Exchange Act.
rules: FINRA Rule 2010 — standards of commercial honor.
FINRA Rule 2120 — use of manipulative, deceptive, or fraudulent devices.
FINRA Rule 4511 — general recordkeeping.
FINRA Rule 4514 — authorization records (no signatures of convenience).
17 CFR 240.15c1-2 — fraud and misrepresentation.
17 CFR 240.15c1-3 — misrepresentation as to registration.
mnemonics: Three 'never' acts = Falsify, Forge, Fail-to-respond (8210).

sections.title: 15. Settlement, Corporate Actions & Option-Exercise Settlement (Errata)
sections.overview: Regular-way equity, corporate-bond, and municipal-bond trades settle T+1 (effective 5/28/2024). When an equity option is exercised, the resulting stock delivery now settles T+1 as well, aligned with the new equity settlement cycle. Index options settle next business day in cash for intrinsic value.
key_concepts: Regular-way settlement for equities, corporate bonds, and municipal bonds = T+1.
U.S. Treasury securities and options settlement (purchase/sale of the option contract itself) = T+1 (options have always been next-business-day).
Equity option EXERCISE → resulting stock trade settles T+1 (post-5/28/2024 conversion).
Index option exercise → next business day in cash (intrinsic value).
Cash settlement = same day (T).
Ex-dividend date under T+1 cycle = ONE business day before record date (formerly two).
rules: 17 CFR 240.15c6-1 — securities transaction settlement cycle (T+1).
formulas: Equity option exercise → stock delivery T+1
Ex-date (T+1 regime) = Record date – 1 business day
mnemonics: 'Everything is T+1' (post-5/28/2024) — equities, corporates, munis, option exercises (stock leg).
